claim: The cohesin complex maintains sister chromatid cohesion from S phase to anaphase onset.
source: The cohesin complex maintains sister chromatid cohesion from S phase to anaphase onset.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, representing established scientific consensus.

claim: Cohesin plays roles in chromosome structure and DNA repair.
source: Cohesin also plays roles in chromosome structure and DNA repair.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about cohesin function.

claim: In yeast, the cohesin subunit Scc1 is cleaved at anaphase onset to allow segregation in an orderly manner.
source: In yeast, the cohesin subunit Scc1 is cleaved at anaphase onset to allow segregation in an orderly manner, although some residual cohesin subunits remain to maintain chromosome structure.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about cohesin regulation in yeast.

claim: Some residual cohesin subunits remain after anaphase onset to maintain chromosome structure.
source: In yeast, the cohesin subunit Scc1 is cleaved at anaphase onset to allow segregation in an orderly manner, although some residual cohesin subunits remain to maintain chromosome structure.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about residual cohesin.

claim: Efficient DNA double-strand break repair by homologous recombination with the sister chromatid depends on cohesin.
source: Efficient DNA double-strand break (DSB) repair by homologous recombination (HR) with the sister chromatid also depends on cohesin.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the role of cohesin in DSB repair.

claim: Scc1 returns in telophase after DSBs.
source: We have found that Scc1 returns in telophase after DSBs and that it partially reconstitutes a chromatin-bound cohesin complex with Smc1 and an acetylated pool of Smc3 after a single HO-induced DSB at the MAT locus.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Scc1 partially reconstitutes a chromatin-bound cohesin complex with Smc1 and an acetylated pool of Smc3 after a single HO-induced DSB at the MAT locus in telophase.
source: We have found that Scc1 returns in telophase after DSBs and that it partially reconstitutes a chromatin-bound cohesin complex with Smc1 and an acetylated pool of Smc3 after a single HO-induced DSB at the MAT locus.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by co-IP and chromatin fractionation data in Figure 2.

claim: The new cohesin in telophase is not required for HR-driven MAT switching.
source: However, this new cohesin is neither required for the HR-driven MAT switching nor binds to the MAT locus after the DSB.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by the Smc3 depletion experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: The new cohesin does not bind to the MAT locus after the DSB in telophase.
source: However, this new cohesin is neither required for the HR-driven MAT switching nor binds to the MAT locus after the DSB.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Cohesin is a multiprotein complex composed in yeast of Smc1, Smc3, Scc1 (also known as Mcd1), Scc3, and Pds5 subunits.
source: Cohesin is a multiprotein complex composed in yeast of Smc1, Smc3, Scc1 (also known as Mcd1), Scc3, and Pds5 subunits (Hirano, 2000; Michaelis et al., 1997; Sjögren and Nasmyth, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Smc1, Smc3, and Scc1 form a heterotrimeric ring that embraces and holds the replicated sister chromatids together and well-aligned until reaching G2/M.
source: At the core of the complex, Smc1, Smc3, and Scc1 form a heterotrimeric ring that embraces and holds the replicated sister chromatids together and well-aligned until reaching G2/M (Díaz-Martínez et al., 2008; Koshland and Guacci, 2000; Laloraya et al., 2000; Michaelis et al., 1997; Strunnikov et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Cohesin subunits are loaded onto chromosomes in G1 by the Scc2–Scc3 complex.
source: Cohesin subunits are loaded onto chromosomes in G1 by the Scc2–Scc3 complex (Ciosk et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: When cells enter S phase, the acetyl-transferase Eco1 acetylates Smc3.
source: When cells enter S phase, the acetyl-transferase Eco1 acetylates Smc3, which inhibits the ATPase activity of Smc1–Smc3 heads and prevents the opening of the Smc3–Scc1 interface (Çamdere et al., 2015; Chan et al., 2012; Huber et al., 2016; Murayama and Uhlmann, 2015; Ström et al., 2007; Unal et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Eco1 acetylation of Smc3 inhibits the ATPase activity of Smc1–Smc3 heads and prevents the opening of the Smc3–Scc1 interface.
source: When cells enter S phase, the acetyl-transferase Eco1 acetylates Smc3, which inhibits the ATPase activity of Smc1–Smc3 heads and prevents the opening of the Smc3–Scc1 interface (Çamdere et al., 2015; Chan et al., 2012; Huber et al., 2016; Murayama and Uhlmann, 2015; Ström et al., 2007; Unal et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Smc3 acetylation embraces the nascent sister chromatids and establishes cohesion.
source: This embraces the nascent sister chromatids and establishes cohesion (Uhlmann and Nasmyth, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The APCCdc20 initiates anaphase by degrading securin/Pds1, so that the separase/Esp1 becomes active.
source: Once sister chromatids are ready for segregation, the APCCdc20 (Anaphase Promoting Complex associated with its regulatory cofactor Cdc20) initiates anaphase by degrading securin/Pds1, so that the separase/Esp1 becomes active.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about anaphase regulation.

claim: Separase cleaves the Scc1 subunit by proteolysis, releasing sister chromatids from cohesion.
source: Separase then cleaves the Scc1 subunit by proteolysis, releasing sister chromatids from cohesion (Cohen-Fix et al., 1996; Michaelis et al., 1997; Nasmyth and Haering, 2009; Uhlmann et al., 1999; Yamamoto et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: The fragmented Scc1 is rapidly degraded.
source: The fragmented Scc1 is then rapidly degraded (Rao et al., 2001), while a pool of Smc1–Smc3 dimers appears to remain through anaphase (Renshaw et al., 2010; Tanaka et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: A pool of Smc1–Smc3 dimers appears to remain through anaphase.
source: The fragmented Scc1 is then rapidly degraded (Rao et al., 2001), while a pool of Smc1–Smc3 dimers appears to remain through anaphase (Renshaw et al., 2010; Tanaka et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The Smc1-Smc3 pool becomes loose as Smc3 is deacetylated by Hos1 in anaphase.
source: This pool, however, becomes loose as Smc3 is deacetylated by Hos1 in anaphase (Chan et al., 2012; Huber et al., 2016; Murayama and Uhlmann, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Some cohesin-dependent cohesion remains at chromosome arms during anaphase, suggesting that residual cohesin is present despite separase activation.
source: Interestingly, some cohesin-dependent cohesion remains at chromosome arms during anaphase, suggesting that residual cohesin is present despite separase activation (Djeghloul et al., 2020; Garcia-Luis et al., 2022; Renshaw et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cohesin can hold two DNA segments within the same chromatin forming an extruded loop.
source: On the one hand, cohesin can hold two DNA segments within the same chromatin forming an extruded loop (Lazar-Stefanita et al., 2017; Rao et al., 2017; Schalbetter et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: DNA double-strand breaks produce damage-induced cohesion (DI-cohesion).
source: On the other hand, DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) produce the so-called damage-induced cohesion (DI-cohesion) (Kim et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Following DNA damage, cohesin is recruited and accumulated both along 50–100 kb surrounding the DSB site and genome-wide.
source: Following DNA damage, cohesin is recruited and accumulated both along 50–100 kb surrounding the DSB site and genome-wide (Ström et al., 2004; Unal et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The cohesin recruitment creates a firm anchoring of two well-aligned sister chromatids, which in turn facilitates DSB repair by homologous recombination.
source: The cohesin recruitment creates a firm anchoring of two well-aligned sister chromatids, which in turn facilitates DSB repair by homologous recombination (HR) (Covo et al., 2010; Hou et al., 2022; Phipps and Dubrana, 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: DNA damage kinases such as Mec1 and Chk1 phosphorylate Scc1 to initiate the cohesion establishment in post-replicative cells.
source: In this regard, DNA damage kinases such as Mec1 and Chk1 phosphorylate Scc1 to initiate the cohesion establishment in post-replicative cells (Heidinger-Pauli et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: HR is a DSB repair mechanism that uses a homologous template for restoring the original broken DNA.
source: HR is a DSB repair mechanism that uses a homologous template for restoring the original broken DNA.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about HR.

claim: HR is highly reliable when the correct template is used, which in mitotic cells is the sister chromatid.
source: HR is highly reliable when the correct template is used, which in mitotic cells is the sister chromatid.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about HR template choice.

claim: HR is the preferred repair mechanism from S to G2/M, when the sister chromatid is available in close proximity.
source: Hence, HR is the preferred repair mechanism from S to G2/M, when the sister chromatid is available in close proximity (Langerak and Russell, 2011; Mathiasen and Lisby, 2014; Symington et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Before DNA replication, in G1, the alternative error-prone non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) is used instead of HR.
source: Before DNA replication, in G1, the alternative error-prone non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) is used instead.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about DSB repair pathway choice.

claim: Cells coordinate the choice of either NHEJ or HR based on the activity of cyclin-dependent kinase (CDK).
source: Cells coordinate the choice of either NHEJ or HR based on the activity of cyclin-dependent kinase (CDK).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about DSB repair pathway choice.

claim: Low CDK keeps cells in G1 and favors NHEJ.
source: Low CDK keeps cells in G1 and favors NHEJ, whereas high CDK is present in S and G2/M and activates HR.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about CDK regulation of DSB repair.

claim: High CDK is present in S and G2/M and activates HR.
source: Low CDK keeps cells in G1 and favors NHEJ, whereas high CDK is present in S and G2/M and activates HR.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about CDK regulation of DSB repair.

claim: In the cell cycle window that spans from anaphase to the telophase-to-G1 transition (late mitosis), high CDK is set to favor HR despite a sister chromatid not being in proximity.
source: Noticeably, there is a paradox in this link between high CDK and HR. In the cell cycle window that spans from anaphase to the telophase-to-G1 transition (we will refer to this window as late mitosis), high CDK is set to favor HR despite a sister chromatid not being in proximity (Machín and Ayra-Plasencia, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Sister loci can move closer and coalesce in late mitosis.
source: In a previous study, we showed that sister loci can indeed move closer and coalesce, and that HR still appears important for DSB survival in late mitosis (Ayra-Plasencia and Machín, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: HR appears important for DSB survival in late mitosis.
source: In a previous study, we showed that sister loci can indeed move closer and coalesce, and that HR still appears important for DSB survival in late mitosis (Ayra-Plasencia and Machín, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: At the anaphase onset, Esp1 cleaves Scc1, opening the cohesin ring and releasing sister chromatids from cohesion.
source: At the anaphase onset, Esp1 cleaves Scc1, opening the cohesin ring and releasing sister chromatids from cohesion.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about cohesin regulation.

claim: After Esp1 cleavage, Scc1 needs to be translated de novo since cleaved fragments are unstable and degraded by the proteasome.
source: Thereafter, Scc1 needs to be translated de novo since cleaved fragments are unstable and degraded by the proteasome (Rao et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Activation of Esp1 can be blocked by DDC kinases.
source: However, it is known that activation of Esp1 can be blocked by DDC kinases (Yam et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: DDC kinases phosphorylate Scc1 to facilitate DI-cohesion at a post-replicative stage.
source: In addition, DDC kinases also phosphorylate Scc1 to facilitate DI-cohesion at a post-replicative stage (Heidinger-Pauli et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: DSB generation in late mitosis can stabilize de novo Scc1 as well as rendering it cohesive.
source: Thus, it is feasible that DSB generation in late mitosis can stabilize de novo Scc1 as well as rendering it cohesive.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on inference from previous knowledge.

claim: Smc1 and Smc3 subunits remain attached to chromatin after segregation.
source: Noteworthy, Smc1 and Smc3 subunits remain attached to chromatin after segregation (Garcia-Luis et al., 2022; Renshaw et al., 2010; Tanaka et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The cdc15-2 allele encodes a conditionally thermosensitive Cdc15 kinase, which drives telophase-to-G1 transition.
source: The cdc15-2 allele encodes a conditionally thermosensitive Cdc15 kinase, which drives telophase-to-G1 transition (Machín and Ayra-Plasencia, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: In wild-type strains, the HO DSB is repaired by HR with the intramolecular ectopic loci HMR and HML.
source: In wild-type strains, the HO DSB is repaired by HR with the intramolecular ectopic loci HMR and HML.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the MAT switching system.

claim: The locus selection for MAT switching depends on the MAT allele (the MATa HO DSB repairs with HML) and results in a gene conversion (e.g., from MATa to MATα).
source: The locus selection depends on the MAT allele (the MATa HO DSB repairs with HML) and results in a gene conversion (e.g., from MATa to MATα).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the MAT switching system.

claim: Scc1 signal disappeared almost entirely when cells were arrested in telophase and remained low in the mock control 2 hr later.
source: The Scc1 signal disappeared almost entirely when cells were arrested in telophase and remained low in the mock control 2 hr later.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Full-length Scc1 was restored after single and multiple DSBs generation in telophase.
source: Strikingly, full-length Scc1 was restored after single and multiple DSBs generation (Figure 1B, E).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1B and quantification in Figure 1E.

claim: Phleomycin treatment increased Scc1 levels fivefold compared to the mock condition, reaching approximately half of the levels observed in G2/M.
source: Compared to the mock condition, phleomycin treatment increased Scc1 levels fivefold, reaching approximately half of the levels observed in G2/M.
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: In the case of HO DSBs, Scc1 levels surpassed those of the mock by more than 15-fold and were even higher than in G2/M.
source: In the case of HO DSBs, Scc1 levels surpassed those of the mock by more than 15-fold and were even higher than in G2/M.
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Smc1 and Smc3 levels remained more stable in both types of DSBs compared to Scc1.
source: In contrast, Smc1 and Smc3 levels remained more stable in both types of DSBs (Figure 1B–D).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figures 1C and 1D.

claim: In asynchronous cultures, both Scc1-3myc and acSmc3 co-immunoprecipitated with Smc1-6HA, indicating that the chromatin-bound pool (acetylated Smc3) of the canonical Smc1–Smc3–Scc1 complex was pulled down.
source: In asynchronous cultures, both Scc1-3myc and acSmc3 co-immunoprecipitated with Smc1-6HA, indicating that we were able to pull down the chromatin-bound pool (acetylated Smc3) of the canonical Smc1–Smc3–Scc1 complex.
evidence: This is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Scc1 was not detected in the pull-down under the mock condition (no DSBs) in telophase.
source: As expected, Scc1 was not detected in the pull-down under the mock condition (no DSBs); however, it was recovered after generation of the HO DSB.
evidence: This is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Scc1 was recovered in the pull-down after generation of the HO DSB in telophase.
source: As expected, Scc1 was not detected in the pull-down under the mock condition (no DSBs); however, it was recovered after generation of the HO DSB.
evidence: This is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Scc1 was not recovered in the co-IP when random DSBs were induced by phleomycin in telophase.
source: Surprisingly, this was not the case when random DSBs were induced by phleomycin.
evidence: This is supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: acSmc3 appeared as two bands in the asynchronous culture but as a single upper band in all telophase conditions, suggesting a difference in posttranslational modifications at this cell cycle stage.
source: Incidentally, acSmc3 appeared as two bands in the asynchronous culture but as a single upper band in all telophase conditions, suggesting a difference in posttranslational modifications at this cell cycle stage.
evidence: This is an observation from the co-IP data in Figure 2A, with an inference about PTMs.

claim: There was an increase in all cohesin subunits in the chromatin fraction after the HO DSB in telophase.
source: To this end, we performed biochemical fractionation of the chromatin-bound proteins, observing an increase in all cohesin subunits in the chromatin fraction after the HO DSB (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by chromatin fractionation data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The increase in chromatin-bound cohesin after HO DSB was approximately twofold for Smc1–acSmc3 and up to sevenfold for Scc1.
source: The increase was approximately twofold for Smc1–acSmc3 and up to sevenfold for Scc1.
evidence: This is supported by quantification of chromatin fractionation data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Chromatin recruitment of cohesin was not observed after phleomycin treatment in telophase.
source: In contrast, this chromatin recruitment was not observed after phleomycin treatment.
evidence: This is supported by chromatin fractionation data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The HO DSB is irreparable in the experimental setup, whereas DSBs caused by phleomycin can eventually be repaired by anaphase regression and sister loci coalescence.
source: In this experimental setup, the HO DSB is irreparable, whereas DSBs caused by phleomycin can eventually be repaired by anaphase regression and sister loci coalescence (Ayra-Plasencia and Machín, 2019).
evidence: This is based on the experimental design and supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The HO DSB leaves clean ends that can be easily resected, while the DSBs after phleomycin are chemically modified and require extended processing.
source: In addition, the HO DSB leaves clean ends that can be easily resected, while the DSBs after phleomycin are chemically modified and require extended processing.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the nature of different types of DSBs.

claim: There was an increase in the Smc3-bound pool around the HOcs in G2/M after the DSB.
source: We confirmed an increase in the Smc3-bound pool around the HOcs in G2/M after the DSB (Figure 2—figure supplement 3); however, such an increase was not observed in telophase (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: An increase in the Smc3-bound pool around the HOcs was not observed in telophase after the DSB.
source: We confirmed an increase in the Smc3-bound pool around the HOcs in G2/M after the DSB (Figure 2—figure supplement 3); however, such an increase was not observed in telophase (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The core of the cohesin SMCs (Smc1–Smc3) is not further recruited to the HO DSB in late mitosis.
source: We thus conclude that the core of the cohesin SMCs (Smc1–Smc3) is not further recruited to the HO DSB in late mitosis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the ChIP data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The lack of local cohesin recruitment to the HO DSB in late mitosis could be due to the inability to increase the acSmc3 pools by Eco1, whose levels drop after G2/M.
source: This lack of local recruitment could be due to several non-exclusive scenarios, including the inability to increase the acSmc3 pools by Eco1, whose levels drop after G2/M (Lyons and Morgan, 2011), as well as condensin binding to chromosome arms during anaphase (Leonard et al., 2015), which might act as an eviction barrier for cohesin loading.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on inference and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Condensin binding to chromosome arms during anaphase might act as an eviction barrier for cohesin loading.
source: This lack of local recruitment could be due to several non-exclusive scenarios, including the inability to increase the acSmc3 pools by Eco1, whose levels drop after G2/M (Lyons and Morgan, 2011), as well as condensin binding to chromosome arms during anaphase (Leonard et al., 2015), which might act as an eviction barrier for cohesin loading.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on inference and supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Reassembly of the full cohesin complex at residual Smc1–acSmc3 dimers may shift the organization of the surrounding chromosome regions and impinge on the HO DSB repair in telophase.
source: However, reassembly of the full cohesin complex at residual Smc1–acSmc3 dimers may shift the organization of the surrounding chromosome regions and impinge on the HO DSB repair in telophase.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on speculation.

claim: Resection is necessary to form the protruding 3′ Rad51 nucleoprotein filaments that invade the donor homologous sequence to restore the break by HR.
source: Resection is necessary to form the protruding 3′ Rad51 nucleoprotein filaments that invade the donor homologous sequence to restore the break by HR (Peng et al., 2021; Symington, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cells in G2/M efficiently resected the HOcs ends.
source: As expected, cells in G2/M efficiently resected the HOcs ends.
evidence: This is supported by resection data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The time to reach half of the maximum resection (t1/2) in G2/M was ~1 hr at 0.7 kb and ~2.5 hr at 5.7 kb from the DSB.
source: The time to reach half of the maximum resection (t1/2) was ~1 hr at 0.7 kb and ~2.5 hr at 5.7 kb from the DSB, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by resection data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Resection in telophase was only slightly delayed at 0.7 kb (t1/2 ~ 1.5 hr).
source: Resection in telophase was only slightly delayed at 0.7 kb (t1/2 ~ 1.5 hr), whereas the delay was more pronounced at 5.7 kb (t1/2 ~ 3.5 hr).
evidence: This is supported by resection data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The delay in resection at 5.7 kb in telophase was more pronounced (t1/2 ~ 3.5 hr).
source: Resection in telophase was only slightly delayed at 0.7 kb (t1/2 ~ 1.5 hr), whereas the delay was more pronounced at 5.7 kb (t1/2 ~ 3.5 hr).
evidence: This is supported by resection data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The delay in resection in telophase may be due to either the fact that CDK activity in late mitosis, though still high, is slightly inferior to that at G2/M or the different chromosome compaction degrees between the arrests.
source: The delay may be due to either the fact that CDK activity in late mitosis, though still high, is slightly inferior to that at G2/M or the different chromosome compaction degrees between the arrests.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on inference.

claim: Rad53 is an effector kinase of the DDC that gets activated by hyperphosphorylation after being recruited to the 3′ ssDNA overhangs.
source: Rad53 is an effector kinase of the DDC that gets activated by hyperphosphorylation after being recruited to the 3′ ssDNA overhangs (Branzei and Foiani, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Rad53 hyperphosphorylation occurred in late mitosis, although with ~1 h delay compared to resection.
source: In agreement with the resection profile, Rad53 hyperphosphorylation occurred in late mitosis, although with ~1 h delay (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The delay in Rad53 activation is consistent with previous studies on Rad53 activation upon an unrepairable HO DSB.
source: This delay is also consistent with previous studies on Rad53 activation upon an unrepairable HO DSB (Pellicioli et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Gene conversion from MATa to MATα can be detected by Southern blot because of a restriction fragment length polymorphism for StyI.
source: This gene conversion can be detected by Southern blot because of a restriction fragment length polymorphism for StyI.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the MAT switching assay.

claim: Cells that are in G1 can barely repair the HO DSB, whereas those in G2/M do so through HR.
source: Cells that are in G1 can barely repair the HO DSB, whereas those in G2/M do so through HR (Ira et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: HO (HO tagged with the Flag epitope) is produced after the β-estradiol pulse and is rapidly degraded afterwards.
source: We confirmed by Western blot that HO (HO tagged with the Flag epitope) is produced after the pulse and is rapidly degraded afterwards (Figure 3D, HO-Flag blot).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Rad53 hyperphosphorylation followed the ~1 hr delay shown in resection experiments and became prominent by the time the DSB inducer had been removed.
source: Rad53 hyperphosphorylation followed the ~1 hr delay shown above and became prominent by the time the DSB inducer had been removed (Figure 3D, Rad53 blot), suggesting extensive resection even in this repairable setup.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Most MATa locus in the cell population has been efficiently cut after the HO pulse in telophase.
source: The Southern blot showed that (1) most MATa locus in the cell population has been efficiently cut after the HO pulse (Figure 3E, F; decrease of the MATa band intensity and rise of that of the cut HOcs); and (2) most DSBs are repaired afterwards exclusively through HR (Figure 3E, F; drop of the HO cut band intensity and rise of that of the MATα).
evidence: This is supported by Southern blot data shown in Figure 3E and quantification in Figure 3F.

claim: Most DSBs in telophase are repaired exclusively through HR after the HO pulse.
source: The Southern blot showed that (1) most MATa locus in the cell population has been efficiently cut after the HO pulse (Figure 3E, F; decrease of the MATa band intensity and rise of that of the cut HOcs); and (2) most DSBs are repaired afterwards exclusively through HR (Figure 3E, F; drop of the HO cut band intensity and rise of that of the MATα).
evidence: This is supported by Southern blot data shown in Figure 3E and quantification in Figure 3F.

claim: No signs of DSB repair by NHEJ were observed in telophase (the remaining MATa band stays constant throughout).
source: No signs of DSB repair by NHEJ were observed (the remaining MATa band stays constant throughout).
evidence: This is supported by Southern blot data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The lack of NHEJ in telophase was confirmed by measuring the repair kinetics of a derivative strain deficient in NHEJ (yku70Δ).
source: This was further confirmed by measuring the repair kinetics of a derivative strain deficient in NHEJ (yku70Δ; Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–C), and is consistent with our previous studies with a HR-deficient rad52Δ strain (Medina-Suárez et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–C and a citation to previous work.

claim: HR kinetics were not altered in cells unable to activate the DDC (rad9Δ).
source: Interestingly, HR kinetics were not altered in cells unable to activate the DDC (rad9Δ; Figure 3—figure supplement 2D–F) or to tether the DSB ends (mre11Δ; Figure 3—figure supplement 2G–I).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D–F.

claim: HR kinetics were not altered in cells unable to tether the DSB ends (mre11Δ).
source: Interestingly, HR kinetics were not altered in cells unable to activate the DDC (rad9Δ; Figure 3—figure supplement 2D–F) or to tether the DSB ends (mre11Δ; Figure 3—figure supplement 2G–I).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2G–I.

claim: The results on rad9Δ and mre11Δ are consistent with previous studies in G2/M cells, in which HR-driven repair of the HO DSB appeared more robust than other types of DSBs.
source: These results are also consistent with previous studies in G2/M cells, in which HR-driven repair of the HO DSB appeared more robust than other types of DSBs (Lazzaro et al., 2008; Moreau et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: HR is the chosen repair pathway in late mitosis.
source: Overall, we concluded that HR is the chosen repair pathway in late mitosis.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The conclusion that HR is the chosen repair pathway in late mitosis is in agreement with predictions based on CDK activity.
source: This is in agreement with predictions based on CDK activity and also fits well with the genetic and cytological data we have obtained before (Ayra-Plasencia and Machín, 2019; Machín and Ayra-Plasencia, 2020; Medina-Suárez et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by inference from established knowledge and citations to previous work.

claim: In cells arrested in cdc15-2, the Smc1–Smc3 pool mostly resides at centromeres where it brings together adjacent regions in both chromosome arms.
source: In cells arrested in cdc15-2, the Smc1–Smc3 pool mostly resides at centromeres where it brings together adjacent regions in both chromosome arms (Garcia-Luis et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The centromeric cohesin configuration could favor the physical interaction in cis of the MAT and the HML loci.
source: Of note, this configuration could favor the physical interaction in cis of the MAT and the HML loci (Piazza et al., 2021), which may in turn promote a rapid and efficient HR-driven MAT switching.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on inference and supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The centromeric cohesin configuration may promote a rapid and efficient HR-driven MAT switching.
source: Of note, this configuration could favor the physical interaction in cis of the MAT and the HML loci (Piazza et al., 2021), which may in turn promote a rapid and efficient HR-driven MAT switching.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on speculation.

claim: The lack of growth in the SMC3-AID* OsTIR1 strain strongly points out that Smc3-aid* is degraded efficiently.
source: Since cohesin is an essential complex for vegetative growth, the lack of growth in the SMC3-AID* OsTIR1 strain strongly points out that Smc3-aid* is degraded efficiently.
evidence: This is an inference based on the spot assay data shown in Figure 4A and established knowledge about cohesin essentiality.

claim: After IAA addition, there was a clear decline in Smc3-aid* levels, including the chromatin-bound acSmc3-aid* pool.
source: After IAA addition, there was a clear decline in Smc3-aid* levels, including the chromatin-bound acSmc3-aid* pool (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: More than 90% of the Smc3-aid* had disappeared by the time the HO promoter was shut down.
source: More than 90% of the Smc3-aid* had disappeared by the time the HO promoter was shut down (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The addition of IAA drastically delayed gene conversion from MATa to MATα.
source: The addition of IAA drastically delayed gene conversion from MATa to MATα (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C), although the cut efficiency was lower than in the wild type in the absence of auxin (~50% MATa remained uncut in the SMC3:aid* OsTIR1 strain).
evidence: This is supported by Southern blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and quantification in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The cut efficiency was lower than in the wild type in the absence of auxin (~50% MATa remained uncut in the SMC3:aid* OsTIR1 strain).
source: The addition of IAA drastically delayed gene conversion from MATa to MATα (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B,C), although the cut efficiency was lower than in the wild type in the absence of auxin (~50% MATa remained uncut in the SMC3:aid* OsTIR1 strain).
evidence: This is supported by Southern blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The detection of DNA damage through Rad53 phosphorylation seems fainter and slightly delayed after IAA addition.
source: Also, the detection of DNA damage through Rad53 phosphorylation seems fainter and slightly delayed (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from Western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In the wild-type strain (no tagged Smc3 and no OsTIR1), the cutting efficiency of HOcs and the yield of gene conversion to MATα were both reduced in the presence of IAA.
source: In the wild-type strain (no tagged Smc3 and no OsTIR1), the cutting efficiency of HOcs and the yield of gene conversion to MATα were both reduced in the presence of IAA, confirming that IAA itself negatively impacts MAT switching (Figure 4C, compared two leftmost lanes with Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by Southern blot data shown in Figure 4C compared to Figure 3E.

claim: IAA itself negatively impacts MAT switching.
source: In the wild-type strain (no tagged Smc3 and no OsTIR1), the cutting efficiency of HOcs and the yield of gene conversion to MATα were both reduced in the presence of IAA, confirming that IAA itself negatively impacts MAT switching (Figure 4C, compared two leftmost lanes with Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: When the yield of the MAT conversion after the recovery time was normalized to the cut HOcs when HO was repressed, no significant differences were observed among the four strains.
source: However, when the yield of the MAT conversion after the recovery time was normalized to the cut HOcs when HO was repressed, no significant differences were observed among the four strains (Figure 4C, D).
evidence: This is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The core of the cohesin complex is not required for the HR-driven repair of the HO DSB in telophase.
source: We therefore conclude that the core of the cohesin complex is not required for the HR-driven repair of the HO DSB in telophase.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the Smc3 depletion data shown in Figure 4.

claim: It was previously reported that cohesin was not required for the MAT switching in G2/M-arrested cells, despite it being essential for efficient post-replicative DSB repair.
source: Of note, it was previously reported that cohesin was not required for the MAT switching in G2/M-arrested cells, despite it being essential for efficient post-replicative DSB repair (Unal et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: HR is molecularly efficient in yeast cells arrested in late mitosis.
source: In this work, we have addressed whether HR was molecularly efficient in yeast cells arrested in late mitosis.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study based on the MAT switching data.

claim: HR is working in late mitosis, complementing previous results that pointed in this direction both genetically and cytologically.
source: We have used the well-established MAT switching system and found that HR is indeed working in late mitosis, complementing previous results that pointed in this direction both genetically and cytologically (Ayra-Plasencia and Machín, 2019).
evidence: This is a primary conclusion supported by the data and citations to previous work.

claim: Residual cohesin, or at least residual chromatin-bound Smc1–Smc3 dimers, are complemented by incorporating de novo Scc1 after DSBs in late mitosis.
source: Our results suggest that residual cohesin, or at least residual chromatin-bound Smc1–Smc3 dimers, are complemented by incorporating de novo Scc1 (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Chromosome structure may undergo significant changes after late DSBs.
source: This fact suggests that chromosome structure may undergo significant changes after late DSBs.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on inference from the data.

claim: Some kind of DI-cohesion could be established after late DSBs, perhaps globally.
source: The nature of these changes remains unexplored, and we cannot currently rule out that some kind of DI-cohesion could be established, perhaps globally.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis.

claim: Telophase chromatin may acquire new intramolecular loops as it occurs in G2/M-arrested cells.
source: Alternatively, telophase chromatin may acquire new intramolecular loops as it occurs in G2/M-arrested cells (Piazza et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: New intramolecular loops or DI-cohesion may favor repair by HR with the intact sister or intramolecularly, although it seems still dispensable for MAT switching at this late cell cycle stage.
source: Either of these may favor repair by HR with the intact sister or intramolecularly, although it seems still dispensable for MAT switching at this late cell cycle stage.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on inference and speculation.
